en.title: How to choose payment methods for your e-shop
en.seoTitle: How to choose payment methods for your e-shop
en.description: Card, bank transfer, cash on delivery or a digital wallet? How to pick payment methods for a small e-shop and which questions to ask a payment provider.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
A customer decides quickly whether an order feels safe and familiar, and the payment methods you offer are a big part of that impression. You do not need every option. You need the few that fit your customers and that you can run without extra work. Here is how I think it through.

The common options

  • Card payment. The default for most online shops. The customer pays straight away and you see the order as paid.
  • Bank transfer. Familiar and simple, but the customer has to pay separately after ordering, so some orders stay unpaid and someone has to track them.
  • Cash on delivery. Some customers still prefer to pay when the parcel arrives. It can help a first-time buyer trust you, but it may come with an extra fee, and a parcel that is not collected costs you the shipping.
  • Digital wallets. Paying with a phone is quick because the card details are already stored there. Whether you can offer it depends on your payment provider.

Questions to ask a payment provider

  • What are the fees, and are they charged per transaction, monthly, or both?
  • When does the money reach my bank account, and how often are payouts made?
  • How are refunds handled, and is there a fee for a refund?
  • What happens when a customer disputes a payment with their bank?
  • Which e-shop platforms does it connect to, and is that connection actively maintained?
  • What is needed to open an account, and how long does approval take?

Keep the answers in writing and compare the total cost, not only the headline rate.

Think about the whole flow

Payment is not just the button on the last step. Decide what happens when a payment fails or the customer closes the window: does the order stay open, and does the customer get an email with a link to pay again? With bank transfer, who marks the order as paid? Where do you issue refunds? These small details create most of the daily work after launch. It also helps if payments match what your accountant needs to see.

Start small

Two or three methods are usually enough at the start: a card payment and one alternative that your customers expect. Add more when you see what people ask for. Show the accepted methods clearly on the product page and in the cart, so nobody is surprised at the end. If customers abandon the order at this stage, read why customers leave the checkout.

en.title: Delivery options for an e-shop: what customers expect
en.seoTitle: Delivery options for an e-shop: what customers expect
en.description: Courier, pickup points or collection in person? How to choose delivery options, set shipping prices and a free-delivery threshold, and set customer expectations.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Delivery is one of the first things a customer checks, often before reading the product description. When the options and prices are clear, the order is easier to complete. Here are the choices I would go through for a small shop.

The main options

  • Courier to the door. Convenient for the customer, but someone has to be at the address or arrange for a neighbour. It is often the most expensive option.
  • Pickup points and parcel lockers. Many customers like to collect a parcel when it suits them. Let them choose the pickup point inside the checkout, so they do not have to look up an address elsewhere.
  • Collection in person. Useful if you have a shop, a warehouse or an office. Give the address and opening hours, and say when the order will be ready.

What you can offer also depends on what you sell. Bulky or fragile goods may only suit a courier.

Shipping price and free delivery

Show the price before the last step. A shipping fee that appears only at the end is one of the most common reasons people give up. Two usual approaches are a flat price per delivery method, or a price based on weight or size.

Free delivery above a certain order value is popular because it encourages a larger basket, but only if your margin allows it. Work it out with your own numbers: the typical order value, the margin on your products and what the carrier charges you. Then show in the cart how much is missing for free delivery, so the customer sees the benefit while deciding.

Set the right expectations

  • State the delivery time for each method, and say from when it counts: from the order or from the dispatch.
  • If you dispatch only on certain days, say so.
  • If an item is not in stock, tell the customer how long it will take before they pay.
  • Send an email when the parcel is dispatched, with a tracking link if the carrier provides one.
  • Explain what happens if nobody is at home and who to contact if the parcel is damaged.

Keep it manageable

Offer only what you can really handle. Every method means labels, packaging, an agreement with a carrier and cases to resolve. Two or three options are a good start, and you can add more when customers ask. If you plan to connect the shop to a carrier's system, it is worth checking early whether the carrier offers such a connection.

The same information belongs on a clear delivery page, which I describe in returns and terms pages for an e-shop. If you would like help setting delivery up in your shop, write to me or see e-shop development.

en.title: Search and filters in an e-shop: when you need them
en.seoTitle: Search and filters in an e-shop: when you need them
en.description: Do your customers need search and filters? When they matter, what to do with a large catalogue, and simple rules for names, attributes and categories.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
In a small catalogue, customers can simply browse the categories. As the catalogue grows, they need a faster way to the right product. Search and filters are that way, but they only work well when the product data behind them is in order. Here is how I think about it.

When you need them

  • A few products in a few categories. A clear menu is enough. A search field still helps people who know exactly what they want.
  • Products that differ by size, colour, material, brand or price. Filters let customers narrow the choice themselves.
  • A large catalogue, or many similar products. You need both, and you need to take them seriously.
  • Customers keep asking whether you have a certain item. That is a signal that it is hard to find.

What makes search work

  • The search box is visible on every page, especially on a phone.
  • It copes with Slovak diacritics, so a search for kozena still finds kožená.
  • It copes with small typos and with the words people really use, not only your internal names.
  • Results show a photo, the price and availability.
  • When nothing is found, the page offers a way forward, such as popular categories or a contact, instead of a dead end.

How much of this you get depends on the tool. The built-in search of a simple platform is often basic, and a dedicated search service can do more, but it adds setup and cost. For a small shop, good data usually matters more than a clever engine.

How to keep filters useful

  • Offer only the attributes people really choose by, such as size, colour, brand and price.
  • Use the same wording everywhere: one value for each colour, not three spellings.
  • Show how many products each choice gives, and make it easy to clear the filters.
  • Hide filters that have only one option.
  • On a phone, put filters in a panel that is easy to open and close.

Simple data rules that help

  • Name products by one pattern: type, brand, model, key attribute.
  • Keep attributes in their own fields, not buried in the description.
  • Keep categories few and group them by how customers think, not by how your warehouse is organised.
  • Use the same units everywhere.

These rules are easiest to apply before products go into the shop, which is what preparing products for an e-shop import is about. A well-built product page also helps, see the product page checklist.

en.title: Google Business Profile: what to fill in for a local business
en.seoTitle: Google Business Profile: what to fill in for a local business
en.description: What a Google Business Profile is, which details to fill in and how verification works. A free step you can do yourself, with no promise of ranking.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
When someone searches for a business near them, Google often shows a box with a map, a phone number and opening hours. That information comes from a Google Business Profile, which used to be called Google My Business. It is free and you manage it yourself. It does not replace your website. The two work side by side.

What to fill in

  • Name. The real name of your business as customers know it. Do not add extra keywords to it.
  • Address or service area. If customers visit you, enter the address. If you travel to customers, you can set the area you serve instead. The rules on hiding an address change, so follow what the profile offers.
  • Opening hours. And update them for holidays and any changes.
  • Categories. Choose the main category that describes you best. Add others only if they are true.
  • Phone and website. Exactly as they appear on your site.
  • Photos. Real photos of the premises, your work and the team, not stock images.
  • Short description. Plainly, what you do and for whom.

Verification of ownership

Google wants to confirm that you are entitled to manage the business. The available methods depend on the business and can change. A postcard, a phone call, an email or a video check are examples of what Google has offered. Set the profile up with an account that belongs to the business, not the private account of an employee who may leave.

Keep it consistent

  • Use the same name, address and phone number as on your website and in your documents.
  • Update the profile when something changes.
  • Answer reviews politely, including the critical ones.
  • Ask real customers for reviews. Do not buy them or write them yourself, because that goes against the rules.

What to expect

A profile helps people find you and contact you quickly. It does not guarantee a position. Google says local results depend on factors such as relevance, distance and how well known a business is, and I cannot change those for you.

Make sure the details on your site match the profile. For the basics of the site itself, see SEO basics for a small website. If you need a new site, read about website development in Bratislava or write to me.

en.title: What to write on the homepage of a small business website
en.seoTitle: What to write on the homepage of a small business website
en.description: A homepage has seconds to say who you are, what you do and how to reach you. A simple structure for the text, and the generic phrases to avoid.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Visitors usually skim a page before they read it. Your homepage does not have to tell the whole story of the business. It has to answer a few plain questions quickly. This is the structure I suggest when a client asks what to write.

Five questions the homepage should answer

  1. Who are you? The business name and the place where you work.
  2. What do you do? One sentence, in the words your customer would use, not internal jargon.
  3. Who is it for? Say who your customers are: households, restaurants, small firms.
  4. What makes you different? One or two real differences, for example a reply within a day or work in one district only. Only what is true.
  5. How can I contact you? Phone, email, address or a form, visible without long scrolling.

An example structure

  • At the top, a headline and a short line saying what you do, plus one main button such as “Request a quote” or “Call us”.
  • Then three or four main services, each with one sentence and a link to its own page.
  • How working together goes, in three steps.
  • Things you can stand behind: real photos, client names with their permission, certificates you actually hold.
  • At the end, contact details and opening hours or the area you cover.

What to avoid

  • Generic phrases such as “we are a dynamic team of professionals offering quality solutions”. They could sit on anyone’s website, so they tell the visitor nothing.
  • Superlatives you cannot prove: “the best”, “number one”.
  • Text that is only about you. Start from the customer’s problem and how you help with it.
  • A long introduction before the contact details, and several equal buttons competing for attention.

A quick test

Show the homepage for five seconds to someone who does not know your business and ask what you do. If they cannot say, rewrite the headline.

I do not write copy for clients, and the text is best prepared by you, because you know your field. What to bring is listed in what to prepare before a website. If you are planning a new site, see website development in Bratislava or write to me.

en.title: Product page checklist for an e-shop
en.seoTitle: Product page checklist for an e-shop
en.description: What a product page needs so a visitor can decide: name, photos, price, availability, variants, delivery, returns, reviews and speed. A practical checklist.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
The product page is where the decision happens. A visitor arrives, often from a search, and wants quick answers: what is it, how much is it, can I get it, and what if it is not right? This is the checklist I use when I build or review a product page.

The essentials

  • Name. Clear and specific. Include what a customer would type into a search: the type of product, the brand, and a key attribute such as size, colour or model. An internal code alone says nothing.
  • Photos. Several images from different angles, and one that shows the scale or the product in use. Photos should match what is delivered. Compress them so the page stays fast.
  • Price. Visible next to the buy button, with a note on whether VAT is included. If you show a sale price, make sure the original price is a real one.
  • Availability. In stock, or how long it takes if not. Do not offer an add-to-cart button for something you cannot sell.
  • Variants. Size and colour chosen on the same page. Unavailable choices are marked clearly, and the photo changes with the colour.
  • Description. The short answer first, details after: materials, dimensions, what is in the box. Use lists for specifications.

What removes doubt

  • Delivery. The cost and time near the buy button, or a clear link to the delivery page. See delivery options for an e-shop.
  • Returns. One plain sentence and a link to the full terms. More in returns and terms pages.
  • Payment methods. Show the accepted ones, so the customer knows before the cart.
  • Contact. A visible email or phone number for questions.
  • Reviews. Show them if you have real ones. With none, it is better to show nothing than to invent them.

The technical side

  • The page loads quickly on a phone. Oversized images are the usual cause of slow pages, as I explain in what slows a website down.
  • The buy button is visible on a phone without long scrolling.
  • Each product has its own address and its own page title, so it can be found and shared.
  • Related products appear only where they genuinely help.

How to use the list

Take three of your best-selling products and go through them one by one, ideally on your own phone. Gaps are easy to spot when you look at the page as a customer. I build the structure of the page and make sure it works well; the photos and the product texts come from you.

If you plan a new shop or want to improve an existing one, write to me or read about e-shop development.

en.title: Redesign or rebuild: what to do with an old website
en.seoTitle: Redesign or rebuild: what to do with an old website
en.description: When a fresh design is enough and when it is better to build the site again: platform, speed, editing, security and new features. And what to keep.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
An old website does not always need to be thrown away. Sometimes a new look is enough. Sometimes the foundation is the problem, and a new design on top only hides it for a while. This is how I help owners tell the two apart.

When a redesign is enough

  • The platform is current and still receives updates.
  • The site loads at a reasonable speed.
  • You can edit texts and images yourself without trouble.
  • The structure and the texts work, the site just looks dated.
  • You do not need functions the site cannot handle today.

When it is better to rebuild

  • Outdated platform. The system or its plugins are no longer maintained, or cannot be updated without breaking the site.
  • Slowness in the foundation. The cause is the way the site is built, not just a few large images.
  • Hard to edit. Every small change needs a developer.
  • Security. Old software that cannot be updated, or repeated break-ins.
  • New functions. You want online booking, an e-shop or a link to a CRM, and the old system cannot take it.
  • Patching costs. Repairs add up to about the price of a new site.

How to decide

  1. Write down what bothers you and what visitors ask or complain about.
  2. Find out what the site runs on and when it was last updated. Your developer or hosting provider can tell you.
  3. Ask for an honest estimate of both options, and a reason why one beats the other.
  4. Compare over two or three years, not only today’s price. A cheap redesign of a weak foundation can cost more in the end.

Sometimes the answer is in between: keep what works and rebuild the rest.

What to keep either way

  • Page addresses. If they change, set up permanent redirects from the old to the new ones, so links and search results do not break.
  • Texts that work, together with page titles and descriptions.
  • Images and logos, in the original quality.
  • Access to the domain and hosting. See who owns your domain, hosting and code.
  • A list of all current pages before the work starts, so nothing is forgotten.

If the old site is an e-shop, moving an e-shop to a new platform covers the extra steps. To talk through your own site, write to me or see website development in Bratislava.

en.title: Returns and terms pages for an e-shop: what customers look for
en.seoTitle: Returns and terms pages for an e-shop: what customers look for
en.description: Delivery, payment, returns and contact pages: what a customer wants to find before buying and how to present it clearly. A practical guide, not legal advice.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Before they buy from a shop they do not know, many customers look for the same few things: how long delivery takes, how to pay, what happens if they want to return something, and who to contact. If those answers are easy to find, the shop feels trustworthy. This article is about that practical side.

This is not legal advice. What an e-shop must publish, and how, is set by law, including consumer rights and the handling of complaints. Please check the exact requirements for your business with a lawyer.

Delivery page

  • The available delivery methods and the price of each.
  • The delivery time, and from when it counts.
  • The order value above which delivery is free, if there is one.
  • Who to contact if the parcel is late or damaged.

More on this in delivery options for an e-shop.

Payment page

List the accepted payment methods, explain how bank transfer works if you offer it (account details, how long you wait for the payment), and mention any extra fee for cash on delivery. Keep it consistent with what the checkout says.

Returns and complaints page

  • How to start a return, step by step.
  • Who pays for the return shipping.
  • How and how soon the customer gets the money back.
  • A form or an address for sending the request.
  • Any goods that cannot be returned.
  • The difference between a return and a complaint about a defect, in simple words.

The exact rights and deadlines are a legal matter, so the text should be checked by a lawyer. My job as the builder is to place it where customers will see it.

Contact and company details

Give the company name, address, registration details, an email address and a phone number if you answer calls. Say when you usually reply. A real name and a real address say more than any badge.

How to present it

  • Link the pages from the footer, the cart and the product page.
  • Put a short plain-language summary at the top, with the full terms below.
  • Use short sentences and headings, so people can find their answer quickly.
  • Update the pages whenever you change a price, a carrier or a rule.

The texts come from you and your lawyer; I build the pages and place them so they are easy to reach. Read also the product page checklist. If you are planning a shop, write to me or see e-shop development.

en.title: SEO basics for a small website: what you can check yourself
en.seoTitle: SEO basics for a small website: what you can check yourself
en.description: Page titles, descriptions, headings, speed, mobile view, sitemap and Search Console: checks an owner can do, and an honest word about rankings.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Search optimisation can sound like a mystery, but a good part of it is basic housekeeping that you can verify yourself. First, to be honest: nobody can guarantee a position on Google, and I do not offer ongoing SEO. What I do is lay the technical foundation while building the site. The checks below show whether it is in order.

Page titles and descriptions

Every page should have its own title, which appears on the browser tab and as the headline in search results, and a short description. A title should say what the page is about, with the service and the place where it makes sense, not just “Home”. The same title on every page is a mistake. Google may show your description in results, but it sometimes picks a different piece of text from the page instead.

Heading structure

A page should have one main heading and sections with subheadings below it. Headings should describe the content that follows. They help readers scan the page and help people using screen readers, which I describe in website accessibility basics.

Speed and mobile view

  • Open the site on your phone over mobile data and watch how quickly the content appears.
  • Text should be readable without zooming, and buttons large enough to tap.
  • A step-by-step check is in how to test your website on a phone, and the usual causes of slow pages are in what slows a website down.

Sitemap and Google Search Console

A sitemap is a file that lists the pages of your site, usually at yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml. Google Search Console is a free tool from Google. In it you verify that you own the domain, for example with a DNS record, submit the sitemap, and see which searches show your site, which pages are indexed and whether there are errors. Looking once a week or once a month is enough.

What to realistically expect

New pages are often found by Google within days or weeks, but positions develop slowly. They depend on competition, content and many things neither I nor anyone else controls. The most lasting thing is useful content that answers your customers’ questions. If someone promises you first place, be careful.

en.title: How to test your website on a phone in 10 minutes
en.seoTitle: How to test your website on a phone in 10 minutes
en.description: A simple checklist for testing your website on a phone: readability, buttons, forms, menu, speed and layout. You only need a phone and ten minutes.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Many of your visitors will open your website on a phone, often while walking or in bright light. A site that looks fine on a laptop can still be awkward on a small screen. You can find most problems yourself in about ten minutes, with no special tools.

Before you start

  • Use your own phone, and if you can, borrow a second one with a different screen size.
  • Switch off Wi-Fi and use mobile data, so you see what a visitor on the street sees.
  • Try the site upright and then turned sideways.

Reading

  • Can you read the text without zooming in?
  • Is there enough contrast between text and background, also in daylight?
  • Do images cut off anything important, such as a headline or a price?

Menu and buttons

  • Does the menu open and close, and can you reach every item?
  • Are the buttons big enough for a thumb, with space between them so you do not hit the wrong one?
  • Does tapping the phone number open the dialler, and does tapping the email address open your mail app?

Forms

  • Does the right keyboard appear, for example one with the @ sign for an email field?
  • Can you still see the field you are typing in when the keyboard is open?
  • Are error messages understandable?
  • Send a real test enquiry and check that you see a confirmation, and that the message arrives.

Speed and layout

  • Does the page appear within a few seconds on mobile data?
  • Does the content jump around while loading?
  • Is there any sideways scrolling, meaning something sticks out beyond the screen?
  • Can pop-ups be closed easily, and do they not cover the whole page?

Write down what you find

Take a screenshot of each problem and note the page and the phone model. That makes it much easier to fix. If many pages feel slow, see what slows a website down, and for contrast and form labels, website accessibility basics.

en.title: Website analytics for a small site: what to measure
en.seoTitle: Website analytics for a small site: what to measure
en.description: Visits, sources, popular pages, form submissions and clicks on phone or email: a few numbers worth watching on a small website, and how not to drown in data.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Analytics tools can show dozens of charts. A small business needs only a few of them. The useful question is not “how many visitors do I have”, but “does the site bring me enquiries”. Here is what I would watch.

Five numbers worth watching

  1. Visits. Roughly how many people come, and how that changes over months rather than days.
  2. Where they come from. Search, direct visits, social networks, links from other sites. It shows which channel actually brings people.
  3. Which pages they view. It shows what interests people, and which pages nobody opens.
  4. Submitted forms. The most important number, because each one is a real enquiry.
  5. Calls and email clicks. Taps on your phone number and clicks on your email address. They are not counted by default and usually need a small setup.

How not to drown in numbers

  • Pick three or four numbers and ignore the rest at first.
  • Look once a month and compare with the previous month, not with other businesses.
  • Write down what you changed, such as a new page or a new offer, so you can link it to the results.
  • Do not react to daily swings. A small site has small numbers, and they move around a lot.

Tools and privacy

Google Analytics is the most common tool, and Google Search Console shows the searches that lead to your site. There are also analytics tools that focus on privacy. In the EU, measurement that uses cookies usually requires the visitor’s consent, so check the rules that apply to you with a lawyer.

What numbers cannot tell you

Analytics shows what happened, not why. Combine it with simple human questions. Ask new customers how they found you, and read the messages that come through the form.

en.title: Why customers leave the checkout and what to do about it
en.seoTitle: Why customers leave the checkout and what to do about it
en.description: Unexpected costs, forced registration, long forms, missing payment options and slow pages are common reasons for abandoned orders. Practical fixes for each.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
A customer who has put something in the cart wanted to buy it. If they leave, something in the checkout got in the way. I cannot tell you the exact reason for your shop without looking at it, but the same causes come up again and again. Here they are, with what to do about each.

Costs that appear too late

Nobody likes a surprise at the last step. A shipping fee, a payment fee or a tax that shows up only at the end feels like a trick, even if it was never hidden on purpose.

  • Show the delivery cost early, in the cart or even on the product page.
  • Show the total clearly, with everything included.
  • If delivery is free above a certain amount, show how much is missing.

Forced registration and long forms

  • Let people order without creating an account. Offer to create one after the order is placed.
  • Ask only for what you need to deliver and invoice. Every extra field is a reason to stop.
  • Use clear labels, and show errors next to the field in plain words. Keep what the customer already typed when there is an error.
  • Test the form on a phone. The right keyboard for an email or a phone number makes a real difference.

Missing options and lost trust

If the customer does not see their usual way to pay or receive the parcel, they may simply leave. Think about which methods your customers expect, as I describe in choosing payment methods and delivery options.

Trust matters too. Make sure your contact details, terms and returns information are easy to find, and that the whole shop runs on a secure connection (HTTPS).

Slow or broken steps

A checkout that hangs, jumps or shows an unclear error loses people quickly, and phones are the most fragile place. Check how fast each step loads (see what slows a website down) and make sure buttons and fields work properly on a small screen.

How to find your own cause

  • Place a test order yourself on a phone and note every moment of hesitation.
  • Ask a friend who does not know the shop to do the same, and watch quietly.
  • Look at the questions customers send you by email or phone before ordering. They point to missing information.
  • If you have analytics set up, check which step people leave at.

Fix one thing at a time, so you know what helped. If you want a second pair of eyes on your checkout, write to me. More about my work is on the e-shop development page.

en.title: Moving an e-shop to a new platform without losing orders or search traffic
en.seoTitle: Moving an e-shop to a new platform without losing orders or search traffic
en.description: A practical plan for migrating an online shop: what to export, how to keep your addresses working, what to test before switching and what to do on launch day.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Moving an e-shop to a new platform is less risky when it is planned as a sequence of small steps. The two things owners worry about most are losing orders and losing the visitors who already find the shop in Google. Both can be protected.

1. List what you have

  • Products, variants, categories and photos.
  • Customers and past orders, if you want to keep the history.
  • Shipping and payment methods, discount codes and tax settings.
  • Connections to other systems: accounting, warehouse, carriers, newsletter.
  • Page addresses (URLs) of the shop.

2. Export and clean the data

Most platforms can export products and customers to a spreadsheet. Use this chance to remove old items and fix names and prices before they move. How to prepare product data is described in how to prepare your products for an e-shop import.

3. Keep your addresses working

If product and category addresses change, set up a permanent redirect (301) from each old address to its new one. Without it, visitors and search engines land on error pages, and the rankings you built can drop. Make a list of the old addresses before you start.

4. Build and test on a separate copy

Work on a test version, not on the live shop. Place test orders through every payment and delivery method, check the e-mails customers receive, and open the shop on a phone.

5. Choose a quiet time to switch

Pick a day and hour with fewer orders. Tell customers if the shop will be unavailable for a short time, and check that orders, payments and redirects work right after the switch.

6. Watch the first weeks

After launch, look for error pages in Google Search Console and fix missing redirects. Compare orders with the previous weeks to catch problems early.

en.title: What happens after your website launches: updates, backups and changes

en.description: A launched website still needs care. What regular maintenance means, what to ask about backups and updates, and how small changes are usually handled.

en.content:
Launching a website is not the end of the work. Software gets updates, content changes and things occasionally break. It helps to agree before launch who looks after what.

Updates

Sites built on a content management system such as WordPress depend on updates to the system and its plugins. Skipped updates are one of the common ways a site becomes slow or vulnerable. Ask who installs them and how often.

Backups

A backup is a copy you can restore if something goes wrong. Ask where it is stored, how often it is made and whether a restore has ever been tested. A backup stored on the same server as the site does not help if the server fails.

Monitoring

Someone should notice when the site is down, when a form stops sending messages or when a certificate is about to expire. Even a simple automatic check is better than hearing about a problem from a customer.

Small changes

  • Which changes can you make yourself, such as texts, photos and blog posts?
  • Which need a developer, and how are they priced: per hour or per task?
  • How quickly can you expect a reply?

Questions to ask before launch

  • Who is responsible for updates and backups?
  • What is included in the price, and what is charged separately?
  • Who do I contact if the site stops working?

en.title: Who owns your domain, hosting and website code?

en.description: Three things should belong to you after a website project: the domain, the hosting account and the code. How to check this before you sign and what to ask for.

en.content:
A common surprise comes years after a website is built: the domain is registered to the agency, or the site cannot be moved because nobody has the files. Ownership is easy to settle at the start and hard to fix later.

The domain

The domain (for example yourcompany.sk) should be registered in your name, with your e-mail as the contact. A developer can manage it for you, but the registrant should be you. Ask for the name of the registrar and check the record yourself.

The hosting account

Hosting is where the site runs. Ideally the account is yours, and the developer has access to work on it. If the account is the developer's, ask what happens to your site if you part ways, and how it can be moved.

The code and content

  • Do you receive the source code and a copy of the content at handover?
  • Is anything built on a licence that must be renewed, such as a paid theme or plugin? Who pays for it and holds the licence?
  • Are the design files yours?

Accounts and passwords

Keep a list of the accounts connected to the site: domain registrar, hosting, analytics, e-mail, payment provider. They should be reachable by you, not only by the person who set them up.

Put it in writing

A short sentence in the quote or contract is enough: what is handed over, to whom each account belongs, and what happens if the cooperation ends. This is one of the questions in how to choose a web developer.

en.title: How to prepare your products for an e-shop import
en.seoTitle: How to prepare your products for an e-shop import
en.description: A short checklist for product data before it goes into a new e-shop: columns, names, prices, photos and variants. Clean data saves days of fixing.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Moving hundreds of products into a new e-shop is quick when the data is tidy and slow when it is not. Most delays I see come from the spreadsheet, not from the code. Here is what to prepare.

One table, one row per product

Keep everything in a single spreadsheet. Each product, or each variant of a product, is one row. Use the same column names for all rows and do not merge cells.

The columns you will usually need

  • SKU, a unique code for every product and variant.
  • Name and a description in each language you sell in.
  • Price, and say whether it includes VAT. Use one format for decimals.
  • Stock, if the shop should show availability.
  • Category, written the same way every time.
  • Photos, as file names or links, one main image and the rest in order.
  • Weight and dimensions, if delivery prices depend on them.

Variants

If a product comes in sizes or colours, decide how to describe them before the import: one parent product with variants underneath, each with its own SKU. Mixing the two styles is the most common source of broken listings.

Photos

Name files so they match the SKU, keep them reasonably sized and avoid text baked into the image. Large uncompressed photos slow the shop down, which I describe in what slows a website down.

Check before sending

  • No duplicate SKUs.
  • No empty required cells.
  • Special characters such as č, š, ž and ľ display correctly when the file is opened.
  • Ten sample rows look right after a test import.

en.title: Website accessibility: the basics every site owner can check
en.seoTitle: Website accessibility: the basics every site owner can check
en.description: What an accessible website means in practice and five simple checks you can do yourself: contrast, keyboard use, alt text, labels and headings.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
An accessible website is one that people can use whatever their abilities or devices. That includes people with low vision, people who cannot use a mouse, and anyone reading on a small screen in bright sunlight. Good accessibility also tends to make a site clearer for everyone.

This article is a practical starting point, not legal advice. For the requirements that apply to your business, ask a lawyer or the relevant authority.

Five checks you can do yourself

  1. Contrast. Text must stand out clearly from its background. Pale grey text on white is the most common problem. Free contrast checkers show whether a colour pair is readable.
  2. Keyboard. Put the mouse aside and press Tab. You should be able to reach every link, button and form field, in a sensible order, and see where you are.
  3. Image descriptions. Images that carry meaning need a short text alternative. Decorative images should have an empty one so screen readers skip them.
  4. Form labels. Every field needs a visible label, not only a placeholder that disappears when you type. Error messages should say what went wrong and how to fix it.
  5. Headings. Use headings in order, one main title and sections below it. People using screen readers move through a page by headings.

Other things worth checking

  • Links say where they lead, not just “click here”.
  • The page works when zoomed to 200%.
  • Videos have captions where speech matters.
  • Nothing important depends on colour alone.

Where to go next

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the common reference for these checks. Automated tools find only part of the problems, so a quick manual pass with the keyboard is valuable. en.title: WooCommerce or a custom e-shop: how to decide
en.seoTitle: WooCommerce or a custom e-shop: how to decide
en.description: When WooCommerce is enough and when a custom e-shop pays off. Questions about products, integrations, shipping and maintenance that settle the choice.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Both options can run a good e-shop. The question is not which one is better, but which one fits how you sell. Here is how I look at it when a client asks.

When WooCommerce is enough

  • You sell a catalogue of ordinary products with variants such as size and colour.
  • Standard payment and delivery methods cover your needs.
  • You want to manage products and orders yourself in a familiar admin.
  • You want to launch sooner and keep the budget lower.

WooCommerce has a large ecosystem of extensions for payments, carriers and accounting, so many needs are met without writing new code. The trade-off is that every extension has to be updated and checked, and too many of them slow the shop down.

When a custom e-shop pays off

  • Prices depend on the customer, the quantity or a complex rule.
  • The shop must exchange data with your warehouse, accounting or CRM in a way ready-made extensions do not support.
  • The ordering process is unusual, for example made-to-order products, bookings or subscriptions.
  • You want full control of the design and the code, without depending on a theme.

A custom build costs more at the start. It can cost less over time if you would otherwise stack many extensions and workarounds.

Questions that settle it

  • How many products do you have and how often do they change?
  • Which systems must the shop connect to?
  • Who will manage the shop day to day?
  • What is the budget now, and what do you expect to change in a year?

  • The booking must connect to your own system, such as an e-shop or a client database.
  • You want the booking to look and behave exactly like the rest of your site.

  • Who owns the customer data?
  • Can the system connect to my other tools?
  • What does it cost per month as I grow?
  • What happens if the provider changes its terms?

en.title: Why website speed matters and what slows it down
en.seoTitle: Why website speed matters and what slows it down
en.description: A slow site loses visitors. What Core Web Vitals measure, the usual causes of slowness and the first things to fix.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
People leave a page that does not respond. A fast site keeps visitors on the page and makes it easier for search engines to read it. Here is what slows a site down and what to fix first.

What Core Web Vitals measure

  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint). How quickly the main content appears.
  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint). How quickly the page reacts when someone taps or clicks.
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift). Whether elements jump while the page loads.

The usual causes of slowness

  • Large, uncompressed images.
  • Too many plugins and scripts, especially from third parties.
  • Slow hosting or no caching.
  • Fonts and effects loaded without need.

What to fix first

Resize and compress images, remove plugins you do not use, enable caching and load scripts only where they are needed. You can measure the result with Google's PageSpeed Insights, which shows these metrics for a given address.

en.title: AI agents are moving into everyday business software: what to prepare for
en.seoTitle: AI agents in business software: what to prepare for
en.description: AI agents that take multi-step actions are reaching business tools. Here is how web studios and small teams can plan for them safely.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
This week, AI company Nous Research announced agents aimed at business users, a sign that “agents” are moving from demos into products companies pay for. The idea is simple: instead of a chatbot that only answers questions, an agent reads a request, uses tools such as a CRM, a helpdesk or a spreadsheet, and completes several steps on its own.

Why agents change the work for web teams

A chatbot on a website is a single window. An agent sits behind it and touches other systems. When you build a website, booking flow, e-shop or internal dashboard, the question is no longer only “what does the page show?” but also “what can the assistant do with our data?”

That raises three practical questions for every project: which actions are allowed, who approves them, and how we can reconstruct afterwards what happened.

A short checklist before you ship an agent

  • Limit the scope. Start with read-only tasks, such as summarising support tickets or drafting replies, before allowing changes to orders or invoices.
  • Use least-privilege access. Give the agent its own API keys with only the permissions it needs, and rotate them regularly.
  • Keep a human in the loop for payments, refunds, legal text and anything that is hard to undo.
  • Log every action. You need a trail of which tool was called, with which input, and what came back.
  • Test with real scenarios. Write 30 to 50 typical and tricky requests, and check the results every time you change a prompt or a model.

What this means for Slovak businesses

Many small companies will not need a custom agent. Their CRM, accounting or e-shop platform will probably add agent features on its own. The studio’s job is to decide where such a feature fits, how it is configured and how the client is protected. The skill that matters is integration and governance, not only prompt writing.

If you want to start, pick one repetitive process that eats time every week, measure it for two weeks, and then test an agent on a copy of the data. The results will tell you more than any launch announcement.

en.title: Do not trust guardrails you have not tested: lessons from this week’s chatbot reports
en.seoTitle: Testing chatbot guardrails before launch
en.description: Two reports this week questioned how well chatbot safety features work for teenagers. Here is how builders can test guardrails before launch.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
This week testers reported that some safety features of a chatbot aimed at teenagers did not behave as promised. One test found the bot kept encouraging users to keep chatting even during a mental health crisis. A watchdog report went further and said some guardrails do not work the way the company describes. Whatever the final verdict, the lesson for builders is the same: a safety statement from a vendor is not a test result.

Why this matters for your project

Many websites and apps now add a chatbot in a few hours. A support bot, a booking assistant or a shopping advisor can receive unexpected messages, including personal, urgent or distressing ones. If the product has no plan for those moments, the harm falls on the user, and on the company that published the bot.

How to test guardrails before launch

  • Write a red-team list. Collect risky and off-topic questions for your domain, including emotional messages, requests for medical or legal advice, and attempts to bypass the rules.
  • Define the expected behaviour in writing. For each category decide whether the bot should answer, decline or hand the conversation over to a human.
  • Add an escalation path. If a conversation suggests a crisis, show the correct local helpline and offer a route to a human.
  • Retest after every change. A new prompt, model version or plug-in can quietly break a rule that worked last month.
  • Monitor real conversations while respecting privacy rules, and review the flagged ones every week.

Age and context matter

If there is any chance that minors will use the product, design for them from the start. That usually means stricter defaults, no open-ended conversations about sensitive topics, and clear information for parents or teachers. Planning this at the beginning is far cheaper than rebuilding the experience after a complaint.

en.title: Bilingual websites in Slovak and English: URLs, hreflang and translations that rank
en.seoTitle: Bilingual SK/EN websites: hreflang and URLs
en.description: How we structure a Slovak and English website so both versions are found, translated well and do not compete with each other in search.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Our own site runs in English and Slovak, and every blog post is now published in both languages. Done well, a bilingual site reaches two audiences. Done badly, it creates duplicate pages, confused search results and clumsy sentences that make a studio look careless. Here is the approach we use.

Give each language its own address

Use one URL pattern for both languages, such as /en/blog/post-name and /sk/blog/post-name. Search engines and visitors can then see which version belongs to which language, and each page has a stable address to share.

Tell search engines which pages belong together

Every translated page should link to its counterpart with hreflang tags, for example hreflang='sk' and hreflang='en', plus a fallback with x-default. The tags tell search engines to show the Slovak page to Slovak users and the English page to everyone else, instead of treating the two as copies.

Keep the slugs in plain ASCII

Slovak letters such as č, š, ž or ô are percent-encoded in URLs, which makes them hard to read, copy and share. Use how-to-choose-ecommerce-platform rather than a long encoded string, and translate the slug as well as the title.

Translate, do not just convert

  • Write native titles and descriptions. A search snippet in Slovak should use the words Slovak people actually type, which are not always a literal translation of the English keywords.
  • Localise the details. Use Slovak date formats, correct quotation marks and number formats, and check every figure and unit.
  • Publish both versions together. A missing translation looks unfinished and leaves visitors without an answer.
  • Review machine translation before publishing, especially technical terms and calls to action.

en.title: Why blog images slow sites down, and how to fix it: formats, sizes and alt text
en.seoTitle: Blog images: formats, sizes and alt text
en.description: Images are often the heaviest part of a blog post. A practical guide to WebP, responsive sizes, lazy loading and alt text, with Next.js examples.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Blog posts without pictures look empty, but pictures carry a cost. A single uncompressed photo can weigh more than the whole text of an article. On a slow mobile connection that means an empty box where the image should be, a layout that jumps around and a visitor who leaves. Good images are part of performance and SEO, not only design.

Start with the right format

Use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF for photographs and illustrations, and keep SVG for logos and simple icons. Next.js can convert and serve modern formats automatically when you use the next/image component, which also resizes each image for the device that requests it.

Give every image a size

An image without a width and height makes the page jump as it loads. Give the browser the aspect ratio, for example with fill inside a container of fixed height, or by setting width and height. Add a sizes attribute so the browser downloads a file that fits the layout, not the largest version.

Load only what is visible

  • Lazy-load images below the fold. Visitors who never scroll down should not have to download them.
  • Mark the main image as a priority when it is the first thing visitors see, so it appears quickly.
  • Compress originals before upload. Export at the size the image is displayed, or slightly larger for sharp screens, instead of uploading a 6000-pixel camera file.

Write alt text and file names for people

Alt text helps screen-reader users understand a picture and tells search engines what it shows. Describe the content in one short sentence, and leave it empty for purely decorative images. A file name such as blog-images-speed-seo.webp is far more useful than IMG_4831.jpg.

en.title: While capital crowds into San Francisco, what should founders in Slovakia do?
en.seoTitle: Founders in Slovakia: capital beyond Silicon Valley
en.description: Endeavor Catalyst has raised $320M to back founders outside Silicon Valley. Practical steps for Slovak and Central European founders.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Investment firm Endeavor Catalyst has raised $320 million to back founders outside Silicon Valley, and part of its profits will go to a nonprofit. The news is a reminder that the best-funded startup scene is not the only route to growth. For founders in Slovakia and the wider region it is a useful signal, but not a shortcut: money follows evidence.

What investors look for outside the big hubs

Funds that look beyond Silicon Valley typically describe the same priorities: a real problem for customers, revenue you can prove, and a team that can grow. Location matters less than the story your numbers tell.

For a Slovak product, that often means selling to customers in Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic or the wider EU from the start. A product that works in a small home market can still become a serious business, but the plan has to show how it will reach more customers.

Five steps for founders in Slovakia

  • Pick a painful problem with a clear buyer. Interview at least 20 potential customers before you write production code.
  • Measure what matters. From the first pilot, track activation, retention and revenue per customer, not only the number of sign-ups.
  • Build for export early. Plan for multilingual content, EU data rules and the payment methods customers in other countries use.
  • Use the local network. Meetups, university programmes and regional accelerators can connect you with engineers, designers and first clients.
  • Keep your website honest. Investors and customers check your website first. A clear product page, case studies and a visible team build trust faster than a long pitch deck.

Money will keep moving toward founders who can show progress, wherever they are based. Your job is to make that progress easy to see.

en.title: Chat is getting visual: three UX rules for AI features on your website
en.seoTitle: Visual AI chat: three UX rules for your website
en.description: OpenAI's new visual ChatGPT interface shows where AI assistants are heading. Three practical UX rules for AI features on client websites.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
OpenAI has launched a new ChatGPT interface with more visual, interactive elements. Instead of only returning paragraphs of text, the assistant can show structured pieces of information that users can explore. For anyone designing an AI feature on a website this is a useful signal: visitors will expect answers they can scan, compare and act on, not walls of text.

Rule 1: show structure when the answer has structure

If a user asks to compare three packages, a table is clearer than a paragraph. If the answer is a date, a price or a list of steps, use the matching component. Visual answers also work better on phones, where many visitors browse.

Do not add charts for decoration. Every card, chart or table should answer a question the user actually asked.

Rule 2: keep actions visible and reversible

When an assistant can filter a product list, book an appointment or change a quote, the user must see what will happen before it happens. Use clear buttons with plain labels, such as “Apply filter” or “Book for Thursday 10:00”, and offer an easy way back. Confirm anything that costs money or sends a message to someone else.

Rule 3: keep a text and keyboard fallback

Visual components are only useful if everyone can use them. Every interactive element needs keyboard access, a visible focus state and a text alternative for charts and images. A good test is to go through the whole assistant with the keyboard alone, and then with a screen reader. If it fails there, it fails for real users too.

These rules also support the accessibility requirements that already apply to many online shops in the EU. We explain them in our article on accessibility rules for Slovak online shops.

en.title: EU AI Act: what Slovak web studios must disclose from 2 August 2026
en.seoTitle: EU AI Act: disclosure rules for web studios
en.description: Transparency rules for chatbots and AI-generated content apply from 2 August 2026. A practical checklist for Slovak web studios and their clients.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Since 2 August 2026 the transparency rules in Article 50 of the EU AI Act apply. For web studios these are the rules that matter first, because they cover chatbots, AI-generated content and certain deepfakes. The rules apply across the EU, including Slovakia, so a studio in Bratislava or Košice that builds for a client in Vienna or Prague can carry obligations too, depending on its role in the system.

What Article 50 asks for

  • Chatbots and voice agents must make clear that people are talking to an AI, unless that is already obvious from the context.
  • Providers of generative systems must mark AI-generated outputs in a machine-readable way, so they can be recognised as artificial.
  • Deployers who publish AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose it, unless a human reviewed the text and holds editorial responsibility for it.
  • Deepfakes of people, images or audio must be disclosed as artificially generated or manipulated.

Law firms that have analysed the 2026 amendment, often called the Digital Omnibus on AI, point to one important transition: systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to add machine-readable marking, while newer systems get no such grace period. The same amendment moves the start dates of many high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028. Check the official text before you rely on any date.

A checklist for studios this month

  • List every AI feature in your client projects, including chat widgets, AI copywriting tools and automated image generation.
  • Add a visible AI notice to chat and voice interfaces at the start of the conversation.
  • Offer labelling options for AI-generated content, and switch them on by default for public-facing text.
  • Clarify roles in contracts. Write down who is the provider and who is the deployer for each feature, and who is responsible for labelling.
  • Keep records of model versions, prompts, reviews and changes, so you can explain decisions later.

This article is general information, not legal advice. If a client runs a high-risk system, such as one used for hiring or credit decisions, get specialist advice early.

en.title: Accessibility is now the law: what Slovak online shops must check
en.seoTitle: Accessibility rules for Slovak online shops
en.description: Since 28 June 2025, the European Accessibility Act applies to online shops. Here is what Slovakia’s rules mean in practice, and a checklist to start with.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Since 28 June 2025 the European Accessibility Act (EAA) applies across the EU. In Slovakia it is implemented by Act No. 351/2022 Z. z. on the accessibility of products and services for persons with disabilities, and by Government Regulation No. 283/2023 Z. z., which sets the requirements for services. Online shops, websites and apps that offer services to consumers are covered, so an online shop is squarely in scope.

What the rules ask for in practice

The goal is that people can perceive, operate, understand and rely on digital services. For a shop that means concrete things: text alternatives for product images, colour contrast that people can read, forms that explain errors clearly, and a checkout that works with a keyboard and a screen reader.

The Slovak rules also expect a shop to make its identification, security and payment functions accessible, to provide accessibility information about the products it sells where it has that information, and to make its support channels accessible.

Who may be exempt

Very small service providers can be exempt. Commentators point to a threshold of fewer than 10 employees and turnover under EUR 2 million, but the exact conditions depend on the wording of the law. Do not assume your client is exempt without checking. Even where an exemption applies, accessible design is far cheaper to build in from the start than to fix later.

A starting checklist for an online shop

  • Run an audit against WCAG 2.1 level AA, the baseline that the harmonised standard EN 301 549 builds on. Combine automated tools with manual keyboard and screen-reader tests.
  • Fix the checkout first. Cart, delivery, payment and confirmation are the steps where people give up.
  • Check colour, focus and text size across the whole theme, not only the home page.
  • Publish an accessibility statement that describes the current state honestly and gives a contact for reporting problems.
  • Keep the theme and plug-ins up to date. A new app or a theme update can break keyboard navigation overnight.

Overlay widgets that promise instant compliance rarely fix the underlying code. This article is general information, not legal advice; check the consolidated text of the law and consult a specialist for your case.

en.title: A software fault stopped a Formula 1 start: testing lessons for every web project
en.seoTitle: Software testing lessons for every web project
en.description: The FIA promised stronger software testing after a fault delayed a race start. Practical testing habits for websites, shops and apps.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Motorsport’s governing body, the FIA, has promised to strengthen software testing after a software fault delayed the start of a Formula 1 race in Malaysia, when cars stopped on the track. Racing and websites have little in common, except one thing: a bug that appears at the worst possible moment costs trust, money and reputation.

The uncomfortable truth about releases

Most failures do not come from exotic bugs. They come from a path nobody tested: a discount code combined with a gift card, a form that only works in one browser, a payment callback that times out at peak traffic. The bigger the event, the more those paths matter.

Testing habits worth copying

  • Test the money path first. Automate the checkout, booking or contact flow end to end, on desktop and mobile, before every release.
  • Keep a staging copy that looks like production. Use realistic content, the same integrations and the same configuration wherever you can.
  • Use a release checklist. Smoke tests after deployment, a rollback plan and one named person who can stop the release.
  • Load-test before campaigns. If a newsletter or an advert will send traffic, test the peak you expect plus a safety margin.
  • Watch errors after launch. Monitoring and alerts catch problems within minutes, before a customer finds them first.

Why this is a business question, not only a technical one

Clients rarely ask how many tests you ran. They ask whether the site will work when it matters. A studio that can explain its testing plan on one page earns trust, and avoids the expensive emergency fixes that follow a bad launch.

en.title: Vertical AI: why software built for one industry keeps attracting funding
en.seoTitle: Vertical AI software: niche markets and funding
en.description: Vesta raised $30M to bring AI agents to mortgage lenders. Why niche B2B software attracts investors, and how small IT teams can pick a market.
en.author: Omnicode
en.content:
Vesta, which sells AI software to mortgage lenders, has announced a $30 million round to bring teams of AI agents into lending work. The story fits a pattern: general AI tools are everywhere, yet investors keep backing products that go deep into one industry. Those products often understand the documents, rules and approvals that a general-purpose assistant does not.

What “vertical” means in practice

A vertical product solves a narrow problem for one type of customer. It knows the vocabulary of its industry, connects to the systems its customers already use and builds in the rules that apply to them. For a buyer, that depth is worth more than a flashy demo.

The same logic applies to smaller projects. A booking system for dental clinics, a stock tool for craft breweries or a quote builder for installers can win customers that a general platform ignores.

How a small IT team can choose a market

  • Start with work you already understand. If your studio has built three e-shops for furniture sellers, that knowledge is a head start.
  • Count the manual steps. Ask ten potential customers which tasks take the most time each week. Repetitive, document-heavy work is the best candidate for automation.
  • Check the rules. Industries with licences, consumer protection duties or personal-data requirements are harder to enter, but they also keep competitors out.
  • Sell a pilot, not a platform. A fixed-price pilot for one process gives you real data, a reference customer and a clearer roadmap.
  • Plan integrations as a feature. Connections to accounting, CRM or payment systems often decide whether a customer switches to you.

Vertical software is not a guaranteed win. It rewards patience, domain knowledge and careful listening, and many web studios already have those skills.

sk.title: Ako vybrať spôsoby platby pre e-shop
sk.seoTitle: Ako vybrať spôsoby platby pre e-shop
sk.description: Karta, prevod, dobierka alebo digitálna peňaženka? Ako vybrať spôsoby platby pre malý e-shop a na čo sa opýtať poskytovateľa platobných služieb.
sk.author: Omnicode
sk.content:
Zákazník sa rýchlo rozhodne, či mu objednávka pripadá bezpečná a známa, a spôsoby platby sú veľkou súčasťou tohto dojmu. Nepotrebujete ponúkať všetko. Stačí zopár možností, ktoré sedia vašim zákazníkom a ktoré zvládnete prevádzkovať bez zbytočnej práce. Takto o tom premýšľam.

Bežné možnosti

  • Platba kartou. Štandard väčšiny e-shopov. Zákazník zaplatí hneď a objednávka sa u vás zobrazí ako uhradená.
  • Bankový prevod. Známy a jednoduchý, ale zákazník musí po objednávke zaplatiť zvlášť, takže niektoré objednávky zostanú neuhradené a niekto ich musí sledovať.
  • Dobierka. Niektorí zákazníci stále radšej platia až pri prevzatí balíka. Pri prvom nákupe to môže pomôcť získať dôveru, no môže byť spojená s príplatkom a nevyzdvihnutý balík vás stojí prepravu.
  • Digitálne peňaženky. Platba mobilom je rýchla, lebo údaje o karte sú tam už uložené. Či ju môžete ponúknuť, závisí od vášho poskytovateľa platieb.

Na čo sa opýtať poskytovateľa platieb

  • Aké sú poplatky a účtujú sa za každú transakciu, mesačne, alebo oboje?
  • Kedy a ako často pošlú peniaze na môj účet?
  • Ako sa riešia vrátenia platieb a platí sa za ne poplatok?
  • Čo sa stane, keď zákazník platbu spochybní u svojej banky?
  • S akými platformami e-shopov sa prepája a je to prepojenie aktívne udržiavané?
  • Čo treba na založenie účtu a ako dlho trvá schválenie?

Odpovede si nechajte písomne a porovnávajte celkové náklady, nielen úvodnú sadzbu.

Myslite na celý priebeh

Platba nie je len tlačidlo v poslednom kroku. Rozhodnite, čo sa stane, keď platba zlyhá alebo zákazník zavrie okno: zostane objednávka otvorená a dostane zákazník e-mail s odkazom na opakovanú platbu? Kto pri bankovom prevode označí objednávku za uhradenú? Odkiaľ budete vracať peniaze? Práve tieto drobnosti spôsobujú po spustení najviac každodennej práce. Pomáha aj to, keď platby zodpovedajú tomu, čo potrebuje vidieť váš účtovník.

Začnite s menším výberom

Na začiatok zvyčajne stačia dva-tri spôsoby: platba kartou a jedna alternatíva, ktorú vaši zákazníci očakávajú. Ďalšie pridáte, keď uvidíte, na čo sa pýtajú. Prijímané spôsoby ukážte zreteľne na stránke produktu aj v košíku, aby nikoho na konci nič neprekvapilo. Ak zákazníci odchádzajú práve v tomto kroku, prečítajte si prečo zákazníci opúšťajú objednávku.

Ak sa chcete porozprávať o tom, ktoré spôsoby sedia vášmu e-shopu, napíšte mi. Prepojenie platieb je súčasťou tvorby e-shopu.

sk.title: Doprava v e-shope: čo zákazníci očakávajú
sk.seoTitle: Doprava v e-shope: čo zákazníci očakávajú
sk.description: Kuriér, odberné miesta alebo osobný odber? Ako vybrať spôsoby dopravy, nastaviť cenu dopravy a hranicu dopravy zadarmo a zladiť očakávania zákazníkov.
sk.author: Omnicode
sk.content:
Doprava patrí k prvým veciam, ktoré zákazník kontroluje, často ešte pred čítaním popisu produktu. Keď sú možnosti a ceny jasné, objednávka sa dokončí ľahšie. Toto sú voľby, ktoré by som pri malom e-shope prešiel.

Hlavné možnosti

  • Kuriér až domov. Pohodlné pre zákazníka, ale niekto musí byť na adrese alebo zariadiť, aby balík prevzal sused. Často ide o najdrahšiu možnosť.
  • Odberné miesta a balíkomaty. Mnohí zákazníci radi vyzdvihnú balík vtedy, keď im to vyhovuje. Odberné miesto nechajte vybrať priamo v objednávke, aby ho nemuseli hľadať inde.
  • Osobný odber. Hodí sa, ak máte predajňu, sklad alebo kanceláriu. Uveďte adresu a otváracie hodiny a povedzte, kedy bude objednávka pripravená.

To, čo môžete ponúknuť, závisí aj od toho, čo predávate. Objemný alebo krehký tovar môže vyhovovať len kuriérovi.

Cena dopravy a doprava zadarmo

Cenu ukážte pred posledným krokom. Poplatok za dopravu, ktorý sa objaví až na konci, je jedným z najčastejších dôvodov, prečo ľudia objednávku vzdajú. Bežné sú dva prístupy: jednotná cena za spôsob dopravy, alebo cena podľa hmotnosti či veľkosti.

Doprava zadarmo od určitej sumy je obľúbená, lebo láka k väčšiemu košíku, no len ak to dovolí vaša marža. Vypočítajte si to s vlastnými číslami: typická hodnota objednávky, marža na produktoch a to, čo vám účtuje prepravca. Potom v košíku ukážte, koľko chýba do dopravy zadarmo, aby zákazník videl výhodu práve pri rozhodovaní.

Nastavte správne očakávania

  • Pri každom spôsobe uveďte dodaciu lehotu a povedzte, odkedy sa počíta: od objednávky alebo od odoslania.
  • Ak odosielate len v určité dni, napíšte to.
  • Ak položka nie je skladom, povedzte zákazníkovi ešte pred platbou, ako dlho bude čakať.
  • Pri odoslaní balíka pošlite e-mail a, ak prepravca ponúka sledovanie zásielky, pridajte odkaz na sledovanie.
  • Vysvetlite, čo sa stane, keď nikto nie je doma, a na koho sa obrátiť pri poškodenom balíku.

Nech je to zvládnuteľné

Ponúkajte len to, čo naozaj zvládnete. Každý spôsob znamená štítky, balenie, dohodu s prepravcom a prípady na riešenie. Dve-tri možnosti sú dobrý začiatok a ďalšie pridáte, keď sa zákazníci opýtajú. Ak plánujete e-shop prepojiť so systémom prepravcu, oplatí sa včas zistiť, či takéto prepojenie ponúka.

Rovnaké informácie patria aj na prehľadnú stránku o doprave, o ktorej píšem v článku stránky s podmienkami a vrátením tovaru v e-shope. Ak chcete pomôcť s nastavením dopravy vo vašom e-shope, napíšte mi alebo si pozrite tvorbu e-shopu.

sk.title: Vyhľadávanie a filtre v e-shope: kedy ich potrebujete
sk.seoTitle: Vyhľadávanie a filtre v e-shope: kedy ich potrebujete
sk.description: Potrebujú vaši zákazníci vyhľadávanie a filtre? Kedy sú dôležité, čo robiť pri veľkom katalógu a jednoduché pravidlá pre názvy, vlastnosti a kategórie.
sk.author: Omnicode
sk.content:
V malom katalógu stačí zákazníkom prechádzať kategórie. Keď katalóg rastie, potrebujú rýchlejšiu cestu k správnemu produktu. Touto cestou sú vyhľadávanie a filtre, no dobre fungujú len vtedy, keď sú v poriadku údaje o produktoch, ktoré za nimi stoja. Takto o tom rozmýšľam.

Kedy ich potrebujete

  • Pár produktov v pár kategóriách. Stačí prehľadné menu. Vyhľadávacie pole stále pomôže ľuďom, ktorí presne vedia, čo chcú.
  • Produkty, ktoré sa líšia veľkosťou, farbou, materiálom, značkou alebo cenou. Filtre umožnia zákazníkom zúžiť výber samostatne.
  • Veľký katalóg alebo veľa podobných produktov. Potrebujete oboje a treba ich brať vážne.
  • Zákazníci sa vás stále pýtajú, či máte nejakú položku. To je znamenie, že sa ťažko hľadá.

Čo robí vyhľadávanie funkčným

  • Vyhľadávacie pole je viditeľné na každej stránke, najmä na telefóne.
  • Poradí si so slovenskou diakritikou, takže hľadanie kozena nájde aj kožená.
  • Poradí si s drobnými preklepmi a so slovami, ktoré ľudia naozaj používajú, nielen s vašimi internými názvami.
  • Výsledky ukazujú fotku, cenu a dostupnosť.
  • Keď sa nič nenájde, stránka ponúkne cestu ďalej, napríklad obľúbené kategórie alebo kontakt, a nie slepú uličku.

Koľko z toho dostanete, závisí od nástroja. Vstavané vyhľadávanie jednoduchej platformy je často základné a samostatná vyhľadávacia služba toho vie viac, no pridáva nastavovanie a náklady. Pri malom e-shope zvyčajne viac než šikovný nástroj záleží na kvalitných údajoch.

Ako udržať filtre užitočné

  • Ponúkajte len vlastnosti, podľa ktorých ľudia naozaj vyberajú, napríklad veľkosť, farbu, značku a cenu.
  • Používajte všade rovnaké pomenovania: jednu hodnotu pre každú farbu, nie tri pravopisy.
  • Ukážte, koľko produktov každá voľba dá, a uľahčite zrušenie filtrov.
  • Skryte filtre, ktoré majú len jednu možnosť.
  • Na telefóne dajte filtre do panela, ktorý sa dá ľahko otvoriť a zavrieť.

Jednoduché pravidlá pre údaje

  • Produkty pomenúvajte podľa jedného vzoru: druh, značka, model, kľúčová vlastnosť.
  • Vlastnosti majte vo vlastných poliach, nie ukryté v popise.
  • Kategórií majte málo a zoraďte ich podľa toho, ako uvažujú zákazníci, nie podľa usporiadania vášho skladu.
  • Všade používajte rovnaké jednotky.

Tieto pravidlá sa najľahšie uplatnia ešte pred nahraním produktov do e-shopu, o čom je článok ako pripraviť produkty na import do e-shopu. Pomôže aj dobre postavená stránka produktu, pozrite zoznam kontrol pre kartu produktu.

Ak váš katalóg rastie a zákazníci majú problém veci nájsť, napíšte mi a spoločne pozrieme, čo sedí. Viac o tom, čo robím, nájdete na stránke tvorba e-shopu.

sk.title: Profil firmy na Googli: čo vyplniť pri miestnom podnikaní
sk.seoTitle: Profil firmy na Googli: čo vyplniť pri miestnom podnikaní
sk.description: Čo je profil firmy na Googli, ktoré údaje vyplniť a ako funguje overenie. Bezplatný krok, ktorý zvládnete sami, bez sľubov o pozíciách vo vyhľadávaní.
sk.author: Omnicode
sk.content:
Keď niekto hľadá firmu vo svojom okolí, Google často zobrazí rámček s mapou, telefónnym číslom a otváracími hodinami. Tieto údaje pochádzajú z profilu firmy na Googli (Google Business Profile), ktorý sa kedysi volal Google My Business. Je bezplatný a spravujete ho sami. Web nenahrádza, obe veci fungujú vedľa seba.

Čo vyplniť

  • Názov. Skutočný názov firmy tak, ako ho poznajú zákazníci. Nepridávajte do neho kľúčové slová navyše.
  • Adresa alebo oblasť pôsobenia. Ak za vami zákazníci chodia, uveďte adresu. Ak jazdíte za zákazníkmi, môžete namiesto toho nastaviť oblasť, ktorú obsluhujete. Pravidlá skrytia adresy sa menia, preto sa riaďte tým, čo profil ponúka.
  • Otváracie hodiny. A aktualizujte ich pri sviatkoch a zmenách.
  • Kategórie. Vyberte hlavnú kategóriu, ktorá vás opisuje najlepšie. Ďalšie pridajte len vtedy, ak sú pravdivé.
  • Telefón a web. Presne tak, ako sú na vašom webe.
  • Fotografie. Skutočné fotky prevádzky, práce a tímu, nie fotobanku.
  • Krátky popis. Jednoducho, čo robíte a pre koho.

Overenie vlastníctva

Google chce potvrdiť, že máte oprávnenie firmu spravovať. Dostupné spôsoby závisia od typu firmy a môžu sa meniť. Príkladmi toho, čo Google ponúkal, sú pohľadnica, telefonát, e-mail alebo video overenie. Profil zakladajte cez účet, ktorý patrí firme, nie cez súkromný účet zamestnanca, ktorý môže odísť.

Držte údaje jednotné

  • Používajte rovnaký názov, adresu a telefón ako na webe a v dokladoch.
  • Keď sa niečo zmení, profil aktualizujte.
  • Na recenzie odpovedajte slušne, aj na kritické.
  • O recenzie žiadajte skutočných zákazníkov. Nekupujte ich ani nepíšte sami, je to proti pravidlám.

Čo môžete očakávať

Profil pomáha ľuďom nájsť vás a rýchlo sa vám ozvať. Pozíciu nezaručuje. Google uvádza, že miestne výsledky závisia od faktorov ako relevantnosť, vzdialenosť a známosť firmy, a tie za vás zmeniť neviem.

Dbajte, aby údaje na webe zodpovedali profilu. Základy samotného webu nájdete v článku SEO základy pre malý web. Ak potrebujete nový web, pozrite si tvorbu webov v Bratislave alebo mi napíšte.

sk.title: Čo napísať na úvodnú stránku webu malej firmy
sk.seoTitle: Čo napísať na úvodnú stránku webu malej firmy
sk.description: Úvodná stránka má za pár sekúnd povedať, kto ste, čo robíte a ako vás zastihnúť. Jednoduchá štruktúra textu a frázy, ktorým sa treba vyhnúť.
sk.author: Omnicode
sk.content:
Návštevníci stránku zvyčajne najprv preletia očami a až potom čítajú. Vaša úvodná stránka nemusí rozprávať celý príbeh firmy. Má rýchlo odpovedať na niekoľko jednoduchých otázok. Takúto štruktúru navrhujem, keď sa ma klient opýta, čo napísať.

Päť otázok, na ktoré má úvodná stránka odpovedať

  1. Kto ste? Názov firmy a miesto, kde pôsobíte.
  2. Čo robíte? Jedna veta slovami, ktoré by použil váš zákazník, nie interným žargónom.
  3. Pre koho? Napíšte, kto sú vaši zákazníci: domácnosti, reštaurácie, malé firmy.
  4. Čím sa líšite? Jeden alebo dva skutočné rozdiely, napríklad odpoveď do jedného dňa alebo práca len v jednej mestskej časti. Len to, čo je pravda.
  5. Ako vás kontaktovať? Telefón, e-mail, adresa alebo formulár, viditeľné bez dlhého rolovania.

Príklad štruktúry

  • Hore nadpis a krátky riadok o tom, čo robíte, a jedno hlavné tlačidlo, napríklad „Požiadať o ponuku“ alebo „Zavolať“.
  • Potom tri až štyri hlavné služby, každá s jednou vetou a odkazom na vlastnú stránku.
  • Ako spolupráca prebieha, v troch krokoch.
  • To, za čím si môžete stáť: skutočné fotografie, mená klientov s ich súhlasom, certifikáty, ktoré naozaj máte.
  • Na konci kontakt a otváracie hodiny alebo oblasť, v ktorej pôsobíte.

Čomu sa vyhnúť

  • Všeobecným frázam typu „sme dynamický tím profesionálov, ktorý ponúka kvalitné riešenia“. Hodili by sa na web hocikoho, a preto návštevníkovi nič nehovoria.
  • Superlatívom, ktoré neviete doložiť: „najlepší“, „jednotka na trhu“.
  • Textu iba o vás. Radšej začnite problémom zákazníka a tým, ako mu pomáhate.
  • Dlhému úvodu pred kontaktom a viacerým rovnocenným tlačidlám, ktoré si navzájom konkurujú.

Rýchly test

Ukážte úvodnú stránku na päť sekúnd niekomu, kto vašu firmu nepozná, a opýtajte sa, čo robíte. Ak to nevie povedať, prepíšte nadpis.

Texty pre klientov nepíšem a najlepšie ich pripravíte vy, pretože svoj odbor poznáte. Čo si priniesť, nájdete v článku čo pripraviť pred tvorbou webu. Ak plánujete nový web, pozrite si tvorbu webov v Bratislave alebo mi napíšte.
